description: Parts 1 to 4A of the Indian Constitution cover the Union and its Territory, Citizenship, Fundamental Rights, Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP), and Fundamental Duties. This forms the philosophical and structural foundation of Indian Polity and is highly crucial for competitive exams.

sections.title: Part I - The Union and its Territory
sections.description: Part 1 (Articles 1 to 4) deals with the geographical boundaries of India, the admission of new states, and the alteration of existing boundaries.

key_concepts.explanation: The Union of India is not the result of an agreement among the states, and the Parliament can alter the boundaries or names of states without their final consent.

polity_articles.provision: Name and territory of the Union
polity_articles.details: States that 'India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States'.

polity_articles.provision: Admission or establishment of new States
polity_articles.details: Grants Parliament the power to admit new states into the Union (e.g., the admission of Sikkim).

polity_articles.provision: Formation of new States and alteration of areas, boundaries or names of existing States
polity_articles.details: Parliament can change the name or boundary of a state by a simple legislative majority (e.g., the formation of Telangana).

sections.title: Part II - Citizenship
sections.description: Part 2 (Articles 5 to 11) deals with the acquisition and loss of citizenship at the time of the commencement of the Constitution (January 26, 1950).

polity_articles.provision: Citizenship at the commencement of the Constitution
polity_articles.details: Provides for citizenship based on domicile in the territory of India.

polity_articles.provision: Persons voluntarily acquiring citizenship of a foreign State not to be citizens
polity_articles.details: Strengthens the principle of single citizenship; dual citizenship is strictly not allowed.

polity_articles.provision: Parliament to regulate the right of citizenship by law
polity_articles.details: Using this power, the Parliament enacted the Citizenship Act, 1955, to govern post-commencement citizenship matters.

important_facts.fact: India follows the concept of Single Citizenship, a feature borrowed from the British Constitution.

sections.title: Part III - Fundamental Rights
sections.description: Part 3 (Articles 12 to 35) guarantees basic civil liberties to citizens and protects them against arbitrary State action. It is often described as the 'Magna Carta of India'.

key_concepts.explanation: Fundamental Rights are legally enforceable. A person can directly move the Supreme Court or High Courts in case of their violation.

polity_articles.details: The State shall not deny to any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the laws within the territory of India.

polity_articles.provision: Protection of certain rights regarding freedom of speech, etc.
polity_articles.details: Guarantees 6 fundamental freedoms. Freedom of the Press is implicitly protected under Article 19(1)(a).

polity_articles.provision: Protection of Life and Personal Liberty
polity_articles.details: No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to the 'procedure established by law'.
Empowers the Supreme Court to issue 5 types of Writs (Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, Quo-Warranto) for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights.

important_facts.fact: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar called Article 32 the 'Heart and Soul of the Constitution'.

sections.title: Part IV - Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP)
sections.description: Part 4 (Articles 36 to 51) contains guidelines and principles for the State to follow in order to establish a socio-economic democracy and a 'Welfare State'.

polity_articles.details: Based on Gandhian philosophy, it directs the State to organize village panchayats as units of self-government.
Directs the State to secure a Uniform Civil Code throughout the territory of India (currently implemented only in Goa and Uttarakhand).

polity_articles.provision: Promotion of International Peace and Security
polity_articles.details: Forms the constitutional bedrock of India's Foreign Policy and its adherence to international laws.

key_associations.extra_info: Unlike Fundamental Rights, DPSPs are non-justiciable (cannot be legally enforced by the courts).

sections.title: Part IVA - Fundamental Duties
sections.description: Added later to the Constitution, this part serves as a reminder to citizens that while enjoying their rights, they must also perform their duties towards the country and society.

historical_events.significance: Added 10 Fundamental Duties on the recommendation of the Sardar Swaran Singh Committee.
Added the 11th Fundamental Duty, mandating parents/guardians to provide opportunities for education to children between 6 and 14 years.

polity_articles.details: Currently specifies 11 fundamental duties, heavily inspired by the Constitution of the erstwhile Soviet Union (USSR).

important_facts.fact: Fundamental Duties are confined only to Indian Citizens and do not extend to foreigners living in India.
